cues.text: Sixty-seven years after the Edict of Milan had merely tolerated Christian worship, the Empire took the further step of naming a single form of Christianity as its official faith.

The intervening decades had seen fierce internal Christian conflict, chiefly the Arian controversy over the divinity of Christ, which the Council of Nicaea (325) had condemned but not extinguished — Arian emperors and bishops still held enormous influence in the East.
Early in 380, the Eastern emperor Theodosius I , a Spaniard by birth and a lifelong Nicene Christian by upbringing, fell seriously ill at Thessalonica .
Seeking baptism as he feared death, he first made certain the local bishop, Ascholius, was no Arian, and was baptized by him into the Nicene faith he had professed since childhood.

Within weeks of his recovery, on February 27, 380, Theodosius, together with the Western emperors Gratian and the young Valentinian II, issued the edict known from its opening words as Cunctos populos .

The edict commanded all subjects of the Empire to hold the faith 'which the divine Apostle Peter transmitted to the Romans,' as professed by Pope Damasus I of Rome and Peter of Alexandria — that is, the Nicene Creed.

It declared: "the religion which was taught by Saint Peter to the Romans" as the standard of true belief, and it branded those who rejected it 'foolish madmen' to be styled heretics , their meeting places stripped of the name 'church.'

Unlike the Edict of Milan, which had protected pluralism, Thessalonica actively authorized the suppression of dissenting Christian creeds — chiefly Arianism, still strong among the Empire's Gothic populations and in parts of Constantinople itself.
Theodosius soon deposed the Arian bishop of Constantinople, Demophilus, replacing him with the Nicene Gregory of Nazianzus.
Path to the First Council of Constantinople

The following year, 381, Theodosius convened the First Council of Constantinople , the second ecumenical council, which reaffirmed and expanded the Nicene Creed into the form still recited at Mass today, and formally condemned Arianism, Macedonianism, and other lingering heresies.
The Edict of Thessalonica marks the formal beginning of Christendom as a legal and political reality: for the first time, one Church's creed became the law of a great empire.

Historians rightly note the edict's harsher, more coercive character compared to Milan's spirit of toleration, a tension the Church would wrestle with for centuries as it navigated the relationship between spiritual authority and civil power.
